bs-equality.name: Balance sheet equation
bs-equality.note: Assets list the uses (what the company owns), liabilities the resources (what it owes).

bs-net-value.name: Net value of a fixed asset

bs-net-debt.name: Net debt
bs-net-debt.note: It is the net debt, not the financial debts alone, that tells you how indebted a company is.

bs-invested-capital.name: Capital-employed analysis of the balance sheet

bs-structure.name: Financial structure ratios
bs-structure.note: Two conditions to finance a large share with net debt: predictable future cash flows and good-quality collateral.

solv-current-ratio.name: Current ratio
solv-current-ratio.latex: \text{Current ratio} = \frac{\text{Current assets}}{\text{Current liabilities}} = \frac{\text{Operating current assets} + \text{Cash assets}}{\text{Operating current liabilities} + \text{Cash liabilities}}
solv-current-ratio.note: Short-term liquidity ratio: know it so you can distrust it. 3-month horizon while the balance sheet is published 3 to 6 months after closing, volatile items, and a WCR increase (mismanagement) can improve it.

solv-quick-ratio.name: Quick ratio
solv-quick-ratio.note: Same criticism as the current ratio: avoid it if possible.

solv-cash-ratio.name: Cash ratio
solv-cash-ratio.note: Same criticism as the current ratio: avoid it if possible.

solv-stable-ratio.name: Medium-term solvency ratio
solv-stable-ratio.note: The critical point is 70%. 100%: ideal · 90–100%: very good · 70–90%: medium but acceptable · 50–70%: high risk of bankruptcy · < 50%: R.I.P. Less strict for companies with negative net debt.

solv-netdebt-cfo.name: Debt repayment capacity (cash flows)
solv-netdebt-cfo.note: Years needed to repay the net debt with all the CFO; must stay below the average maturity of the debt (≈ 3 years). 0–1 year: excellent · 1–2: good · 2–3: medium but acceptable · 3–5: high risk of bankruptcy · > 5: R.I.P.

solv-netdebt-ebitda.name: Net debt / EBITDA leverage
solv-netdebt-ebitda.note: Not as good as net debt / CFO (ignores the WCR change) but quick to compute. Below 3: no problem · up to 4: OK · above 5: high risk of bankruptcy.

is-result.name: Result
is-result.note: A profit if income exceeds expenses, a loss otherwise.

is-expenses.name: Cash and calculated items
is-expenses.note: Calculated expenses: depreciation and provision allowances. They reduce the result without any cash going out.

symbols.meaning: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization

is-financial.name: Financial result
is-financial.note: It reflects the cost of the company's net debt.

is-nonrecurring.name: Non-recurring result
is-nonrecurring.note: Not recognised by IFRS since the 1990s nor by US GAAP since 2015: move it to operating items if it comes back every year.

is-production.name: Production of the period
is-production.note: Finished goods in inventory are valued at production cost, not at selling price.

is-breakeven.name: Break-even point
is-breakeven.latex: \text{Break-even point} = \frac{\text{Fixed costs}}{\text{Margin on variable cost in \%}} \quad \text{with} \quad \text{Margin on variable cost} = \frac{\text{Sales} - \text{Variable costs}}{\text{Sales}}
is-breakeven.note: The higher the fixed costs, the higher the break-even point and the more the result reacts to a drop in turnover.

wcr-def.name: Working Capital Requirement (WCR)
wcr-def.note: Each item has a short life, but their aggregate is stable: a permanent need, to be financed by stable resources. WCR > 0: a need; WCR < 0: a resource.

wcr-approx.name: WCR, usual approximation
wcr-approx.note: Approximation: trade receivables and trade payables make up most of operating receivables and payables.

wcr-net-cash.name: Net cash
wcr-net-cash.note: Ideally close to zero. Very positive: cash that "sleeps". Negative: the bank tolerates it up to a point, then comes the risk of bankruptcy.

cf-cfo-indirect.name: Cash flows from operations, indirect method
cf-cfo-indirect.note: A WCR increase (higher receivables or inventories, lower trade payables) consumes cash.

prof-general.name: Profitability (general case)
prof-general.latex: \text{Profitability} = \frac{\text{Wealth creation (profit)}}{\text{Capital invested to get this gain}}

prof-nopat.name: Economic profit after tax (NOPAT)
prof-nopat.note: If there is a non-recurring result, add it to the EBIT.

prof-roce.name: Economic profitability (ROCE)
prof-roce.note: Independent of the financial structure. Compare it to the WACC: ROCE > WACC, value creation; ROCE < WACC, value destruction.

prof-kd.name: Cost of net debt after tax
prof-kd.note: Net financial expenses = interest on financial debts − financial income from the cash assets.

prof-leverage.name: Financial leverage effect

symbols.meaning: Cost of net debt after tax

prof-leverage.note: If ROCE > kD, debt boosts the ROE. If ROCE < kD, the effect turns negative and amplifies the fall. And when D/E rises, the lender's risk rises, so does kD.

symbols.meaning: Net financial expenses after tax effect

wacc-def.name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)

symbols.meaning: Net debt = financial debts − cash assets
Cost of equity (shareholders' required minimum profitability)
Cost of net debt after tax

wacc-def.note: The minimum rate of return on investments that satisfies both shareholders and debtholders.

wacc-kd.name: Tax effect on the cost of debt

symbols.meaning: Average interest rate on net debt before tax

wacc-kd.note: Interest on loans is deductible from corporate tax.

wacc-value.name: Value creation or destruction
wacc-value.note: A positive net profit is not enough: it must cover the return required for the risk borne by the shareholder.

wacc-market-values.name: Market values (perpetuity of the course example)
wacc-market-values.latex: V_E = \frac{\text{Net profit}}{k_E} \qquad V_D = \frac{\text{Net financial expenses}}{k_D} \qquad \text{Goodwill} = V_E - \text{Book value of equity}

symbols.meaning: Equity beta: slope of the regression of the stock on the market

wacc-market.name: WACC at market values
wacc-market.note: E = market capitalisation, D = market value of net debt, kD before tax.

npv-discounting.name: Discounting
npv-discounting.note: The more distant the flow, or the higher the required rate, the lower its present value.

npv-def.name: Net Present Value (NPV)

symbols.meaning: Absolute value of the initial investment
Discount rate = required return (WACC for a typical project)

npv-def.note: NPV > 0: the project creates value, go. NPV < 0: STOP. Among mutually exclusive projects, pick the highest NPV.

irr-def.name: Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
irr-def.note: IRR > required rate: value creation. Drawbacks: sometimes no solution or several, and a bad criterion to rank mutually exclusive projects (use the NPV).

npv-fcff.name: Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF)
npv-fcff.note: FCFF exclude financing flows: the cost of financing is already in the discount rate.

npv-payback.name: Payback period
npv-payback.latex: \text{Payback} = t \;\text{such that}\; \sum_{k=0}^{t} F_k = 0 \quad \text{(cumulated flows, initial outlay included)}
npv-payback.note: Ignores the time value of money and the flows after the payback: compare it to a sector reference, never use it alone.

val-ev-dcf.name: Enterprise value by DCF
val-ev-dcf.note: Gordon-Shapiro, valid if WACC > g. Equity value = EV − net debt.

cf-cfo-direct.name: Cash flows from operations, direct method
cf-cfo-direct.note: Cash-in: payments from clients. Cash-out: payments to suppliers, salaries, etc.

cf-cfi.name: Cash flows from investments (CFI)
cf-cfi.latex: \text{CFI} = -\,\text{Acquisitions of fixed assets} + \text{Disposals of fixed assets}
cf-cfi.note: Investments in new fixed assets, minus the fixed assets sold during the period.

cf-cff.name: Cash flows from financing (CFF)
cf-cff.latex: \begin{aligned}\text{CFF} = &+ \text{New loan emission} - \text{Loan capital reimbursement} - \text{Interest payment} \\ &+ \text{Social capital increase} - \text{Social capital decrease} - \text{Dividends}\end{aligned}
cf-cff.note: Flows from or to capital providers: lenders (new loans, repayments, interest) and shareholders (capital, dividends).

cf-fcff.name: Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF)
cf-fcff.note: The cash the company has at its disposal once the necessary investments are paid: repay debts, pay a dividend, keep cash. For a valuation, take the FCFF before financial interests.

cf-cfo-net-profit.name: Cash flows from operations, starting from net profit
cf-cfo-net-profit.latex: \text{CFO after interest paid} = \text{Net profit} + \text{Depreciation and provision allowances} - \Delta\,\text{WCR}
cf-cfo-net-profit.note: The most common presentation, but interest stays in the operating flows; purists move it to the financing flows, with tax computed on EBIT.

solv-cessation.name: Cessation of payments
solv-cessation.note: The company can no longer immediately meet its liabilities due with its available assets: it enters collective proceedings (receivership or judicial liquidation), the French "dépôt de bilan". In France, it must be declared to the court within 45 days.

val-three-steps.name: Equity value, in 3 steps

symbols.meaning: Market value of the net financial debt (step 2)
Market value of equity, by difference (step 3)

val-three-steps.note: We do not value equity directly (apart from a few sectors like banking). The financial structure has no impact on the value of the assets: the size of the pizza does not depend on how it is sliced.

val-ev-def.name: Enterprise value
val-ev-def.latex: \text{EV} = \text{MV of capital employed} = \text{MV of equity} + \text{MV of net financial debt}
val-ev-def.note: MV: market value. A book value is not a market value. "Price is what you pay; value is what you get": the price depends on the intrinsic value and on the synergies the buyer is ready to pay for.

val-terminal.name: Terminal value (Gordon-Shapiro)

symbols.meaning: Perpetual growth rate of the flows beyond the explicit horizon
Last year of the explicit horizon

val-terminal.note: Only valid if WACC > g. As g gets close to the WACC, the value goes to infinity: g must stay reasonable (long-term inflation, for instance). Demonstration p. 450.

val-multiples.name: Multiples method
val-multiples.note: Three steps: sample of peers (same risk, same growth), choice of multiple, reference year. Favour EV multiples, and among them EV / EBIT: the P/E is distorted by the financial structure, EV / Sales ignores profitability, EV / EBITDA "normalises" capital intensity. Then V_E = EV − net debt.

val-ddm.name: Dividend Discount Model (DDM)

symbols.meaning: Dividend expected one year from now

val-ddm.note: Dividends go to shareholders: discount them at the cost of equity, not at the WACC. Absurd results as g gets close to kE, and negative ones if g > kE.

mkt-stock-value.name: Value of a stock

symbols.meaning: Cash flows attached to the stock (FCFF minus cash flows for lenders), uncertain
Discount rate: risk-free rate + risk premium of the stock
Delay between the calculation date and the cash flow

mkt-stock-value.note: Delayed flows or rising rates: the price falls. A competitor withdrawing or a takeover bid with synergies: it rises.

mkt-bond-value.name: Value of a bond

symbols.meaning: Interest and capital redemption, known at issuance
Risk-free rate + risk premium of the issuer

mkt-bond-value.note: At a fixed rate, if rates rise or the issuer is downgraded, i increases and the price falls. At a variable rate, flows and i move together: no impact. A lower dividend changes nothing for the lender.

mkt-future.name: Futures or forward contract (buyer)
mkt-future.latex: \text{Buyer's gain} = Q \times (p - F) \qquad \begin{cases} p > F : \text{gain} \\ p < F : \text{loss} \end{cases}
mkt-future.note: A firm, reciprocal commitment: the seller makes exactly the opposite. For the hedged buyer, spot purchase − gain on the contract = Q × F, whatever p. Futures: organised market, clearing house, initial margin and margin calls. Forwards: over the counter, counterparty risk.

mkt-call.name: Call option, at maturity

symbols.meaning: Value of the underlying asset at maturity

mkt-call.note: A right, not an obligation: exercised only if S > K ("in the money"). The premium is paid upfront whatever happens: the buyer's loss is limited to the premium, the seller's is potentially unlimited. Before maturity, a time value is added.

mkt-put.name: Put option, at maturity
mkt-put.note: The right, but not the obligation, to sell at the strike price: a protection against a fall. The course defines the put (p. 498); same logic as the call, mirrored.

su-investor-share.name: Share of the new investors

symbols.meaning: Market value of equity after the capital increase (post-money), negotiated

su-investor-share.note: In this order: 1. the entrepreneur estimates the cash need INV; 2. entrepreneur and investors negotiate the POST value (DCF, multiples…); 3. investors receive INV / POST of the new share capital; 4. the remainder goes to the share premium.

su-capital-increase.name: Increase in share capital

symbols.meaning: Increase in share capital (new shares × nominal value)

su-capital-increase.note: Course example: €10k × 90 / 112.5 = €8k, i.e. 8 new shares with a €1,000 nominal value, issued at €11,250 each.

su-share-premium.name: Share premium
su-share-premium.note: The €90k raised do not give 90% of the power: €8k go to share capital, €82k to the share premium, on the liabilities side.

su-power.name: Sharing of power
su-power.note: The split of share capital determines the split of power. Course example: 10 / 18 = 56% for the entrepreneur, 44% for the new shareholders.

rs-restructuring.name: Restructuring when ROCE < WACC
rs-restructuring.latex: \text{ROCE} < \text{WACC} \Rightarrow \begin{cases} \nearrow \text{economic result: higher sales, lower costs} \\ \searrow \text{WACC: very difficult} \end{cases}
rs-restructuring.note: Otherwise investors turn away, or a competitor launches a takeover bid. The WACC pre-exists the financial structure: it only depends on the business risk. The only lever on that side: more transparent financial communication.

bk-priority.name: Order of repayment in liquidation
bk-priority.note: General order, which varies across countries. Shareholders come last: on average they recover close to 0%. No debt, no bankruptcy… but value can still be destroyed if ROCE < WACC.
